heading: Background
html:
Most childhood musculoskeletal presentations are benign and self-resolving, but a small number (septic arthritis, slipped upper femoral epiphysis (SUFE), Perthes disease, malignancy, non-accidental injury) are time-critical. Age is the strongest discriminator in the limping child:

  • 0–3 years: septic arthritis/osteomyelitis, developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH), toddler's fracture, NAI
  • 3–10 years: transient synovitis ('irritable hip'), Perthes disease, septic arthritis
  • 10–16 years: SUFE, Osgood-Schlatter, stress fracture, inflammatory arthritis

heading: Assessment
html:
Red flags in the limping child — same-day assessment

  • Fever or systemic upset (septic arthritis until excluded)
  • Unable to weight bear
  • Age under 3 with a limp (low threshold — poor localisers, NAI window)
  • Night pain, weight loss, fatigue or pallor (malignancy)
  • Pain out of proportion, or history inconsistent with injury (NAI)
  • Adolescent with hip pain, thigh or knee pain, or an externally rotated limp — SUFE until excluded
  • Examine the hip in every 'knee pain' — SUFE and Perthes classically present with knee or thigh pain.
  • Transient synovitis is a diagnosis of exclusion: well child, afebrile, weight bearing (perhaps with a limp), often after a viral illness.
  • DDH: asymmetrical skin creases, limited abduction, leg length difference, waddling gait in the walker.
  • Scoliosis: forward bend test; assess for pain, rapid progression, neurological symptoms.

heading: Primary care management
html:
Normal variants — reassure and demonstrate (no imaging, no referral when criteria met):

  • Flexible flat feet: arch reforms on tiptoe standing; painless — normal into mid-childhood.
  • In-toeing (femoral anteversion, tibial torsion, metatarsus adductus): symmetrical and improving with growth — resolves in the vast majority by 8–10 years.
  • Bow legs (genu varum): normal up to ~3 years. Knock knees (genu valgum): normal ~2–7 years.
  • Curly toes: common, familial, rarely need anything.

Common self-limiting conditions:

  • Transient synovitis: rest, simple analgesia, review in 48 hours and safety-net (return if fever, worsening, not resolving in 1–2 weeks).
  • Osgood-Schlatter / Sever's disease: activity modification, analgesia, reassurance — settles with skeletal maturity.
  • Growing pains: bilateral, evening/night, normal examination, no limp, no daytime symptoms — reassure; any red flag feature makes this diagnosis unsafe.

heading: Who to refer
html:
Same-day (paediatrics / orthopaedics on call / ED)

  • Limping child with fever or systemic upset
  • Non-weight-bearing child
  • Suspected SUFE — keep non-weight-bearing while arranging same-day assessment
  • Limp in a child under 3
  • Suspected NAI — follow child protection procedures

Urgent (SCI Gateway)

  • Suspected Perthes disease (persistent limp/hip pain age 3–10; X-ray hips including frog lateral)
  • Suspected DDH beyond the newborn screening window — X-ray (or ultrasound <4½ months) and refer
  • Persistent unexplained limp >2 weeks despite normal initial workup
  • Painful, rapidly progressive scoliosis or scoliosis with neurological signs

Routine

  • Rigid or painful flat foot
  • Asymmetrical, progressive or painful rotational/angular variants, or those outside age norms
  • Adolescent idiopathic scoliosis without red flags but with progression or significant deformity

heading: Who not to refer
html:
• Symmetrical, painless normal variants within age norms: flexible flat feet, in-toeing, bow legs (<3 years), knock knees (2–7 years), curly toes — reassure, review if progressive or painful.
  • Classic growing pains with a normal examination.
  • Osgood-Schlatter and Sever's disease — manage in primary care.
  • Resolved transient synovitis in a well child.
